confidence_note: Recalled from the book and well-known sources, not page-checked: surgeons in blood-stiffened coats; Lister in Glasgow reading Pasteur; carbolic acid used on sewage; August 1865 case of James Greenlees, an eleven-year-old boy with a compound leg fracture treated with carbolic dressings and recovering. Omitted as unverified: exact dates of the dressing changes, mortality statistics, the carbolic spray, names of the mockers. Old text's claim about numbers of later surgeries dropped. Liston and Condy's fluid/Carlisle details from a study guide and Wikipedia; the 28 seconds is the study guide's figure.
facts: In the mid-1800s surgery was done without any idea of germs; some surgeons wore coats stiff with old blood as a mark of experience.
Wounds often turned septic after an operation, and patients died of infections nobody could explain.
Joseph Lister, a surgeon in Glasgow, read Louis Pasteur's work showing that microscopic organisms cause putrefaction.
Carbolic acid had been used to treat sewage; Lister reasoned it might kill the organisms in a wound.
In August 1865 he treated an eleven-year-old boy, James Greenlees, whose leg had a compound fracture (bone through the skin), by dressing it with carbolic acid.
The wound did not turn septic and the boy's leg healed.
Other surgeons doubted that invisible organisms mattered and resisted his methods for years.
The book opens with Robert Liston, a surgeon famous for speed, and a December 1846 mid-thigh amputation in about half a minute (a study-guide summary gives 28 seconds).
Surgeons took pride in unwashed, stained gowns; one phrase for it was the good old surgical stink.

Before 1865 Lister tried a household disinfectant, Condy's fluid, and the limb still festered; then he heard that carbolic acid, a relative of creosote, was used to treat sewage in Carlisle and got a sample.
scene_details: a coat stiff with dried blood
a boy's broken leg with the bone through the skin
tension: A wound that normally killed was treated against an enemy nobody could see.
opening_idea: Open on the stiff, blood-caked coat a surgeon wore with pride.

lessons.idea: A cause you cannot see can still be acted on; treat the invisible one as real when the evidence points to it.
lessons.anchor: Lister acted on Pasteur's invisible organisms with carbolic acid

reflect_final: Which problem in your own work keeps coming back with no visible cause, and what invisible factor could you test for next time it appears?

use_cases.situation: A recurring error keeps reaching customers.
use_cases.move: Propose a short review of the step nobody checks, the way Lister cleaned what he could not see.

use_cases.situation: A colleague shrugs off a small hygiene or safety step.
use_cases.move: Ask them to try it for two weeks and compare what happens.

use_cases.situation: You keep getting sick after the same kind of family event.
use_cases.move: Look at what is shared there, like food or surfaces, and change one thing.

pocket_idea: Lister dressed a boy's open fracture with carbolic acid against germs no one could see; clean the step you can't see failing.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Surgeons wore blood-stiff coats with pride while Lister cleaned wounds against germs nobody could see.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: In Glasgow in 1865 Joseph Lister read Pasteur's work on microscopic organisms. When an eleven-year-old boy came in with a compound leg fracture, Lister dressed it with carbolic acid. The wound stayed clean and the leg healed, though many surgeons still resisted for years.
